```{r}
#| label: setup
# The report never retypes a result. It reads the files comparison/run.R writes
# (comparison/export/r/*.csv) and the two analyses' export contracts. The functions in
# comparison/R/ are sourced so the folds can show their code, and so a few lines below
# can recompute the two main estimates from the contracts and check them against the export.
for (f in list.files("../R", pattern = "[.]R$", full.names = TRUE)) source(f, keep.source = TRUE)
root <- comparison_root()
ex <- read_exports(file.path(root, "comparison", "export", "r"))   # R/site.R
k  <- read_contracts(root)                                          # R/contract.R
ep <- ex$endpoints; en <- ex$ends; br <- ex$bridge; inp <- ex$inputs
# the dial path: the explorer's dials moved in the equation's order, each to its far end (R/model.R)
dp <- read_csv_plain(file.path(root, "comparison", "export", "r", "dial_path.csv"))
own <- en[en$horizon_setting == "own", ]
ea <- own[own$output == "a", ]; eb <- own[own$output == "b", ]
epv <- function(id, col = "value") ep[[col]][ep$endpoint_id == id]
steps <- bridge_steps()
# The discount rate at each end (the rate dial, author decision 2026-10-15) and the JR
# analysis's draw range, from the export
mv <- function(key) ex$meta$value[ex$meta$key == key]
r3 <- rate_txt(mv("r_bsz")); r_jr <- rate_txt(mv("r_jr"))
r_lo <- pct(mv("r_min_jr"), 1); r_hi <- pct(mv("r_max_jr"), 1)
# The three largest steps averaged over every order (the Shapley check), on output (b) at each
# analysis's own horizon, and the three largest on the explorer's path. The introduction names
# both lists in words (the path's ranking depends on its order); stop if either changes.
b_own_b <- br[br$horizon_setting == "own" & br$output == "b", ]
shap3_ids <- b_own_b$step_id[order(-abs(b_own_b$shapley))][1:3]
path3_ids <- dp$step_id[order(-abs(dp$change))][1:3]
stopifnot(setequal(path3_ids, c("horizon", "litigation_survival", "confirmed_departures")),
          setequal(shap3_ids, c("litigation_survival", "income_loss_share", "horizon")))
# A(H, r): what 1 a year for H years is worth today at the rate r
# A signed amount stays on one line: a browser may break a line between a minus sign and the
# dollar sign, so amounts are wrapped in a no-wrap span, in running text (usd()) and in the
# tables (show(), which also catches amounts inside the source texts).
nobr <- function(x) ifelse(nzchar(x), sprintf('<span style="white-space:nowrap">%s</span>', x), x)
nobr_amounts <- function(x) gsub("([\u2212+-]\\$[0-9][0-9,.]*B)", '<span style="white-space:nowrap">\\1</span>', x)
# Money in running text: a dollar sign in markdown starts a formula, so escape it.
usd <- function(x, d = 1, signed = FALSE) nobr(gsub("$", "\\$", money(x, d, signed), fixed = TRUE))
# The BSZ authors' rounded headline ("about $100 billion", the abstract's rounding of Table 5's
# $104 billion; the endpoint ggss_headline holds the same rounding), as the root page words it.
bsz_round_words <- nobr(sprintf("\\$%s billion", format(epv("ggss_headline"))))
# Two pandoc traps in raw HTML tables: a bare dollar sign can pair with the next one into
# a formula across cells, and "(a)" in a cell reads as a list marker that leaves the
# surrounding <div> unclosed. Every table writes both as HTML entities.
ent <- function(x) gsub("\\(([a-z])\\)", "&#40;\\1)", gsub("$", "&#36;", x, fixed = TRUE))
show <- function(df) {
  df[] <- lapply(df, function(x) if (is.character(x)) ent(nobr_amounts(x)) else x)
  names(df) <- ent(names(df))
  knitr::kable(df, format = "html", escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, table.attr = 'class="table table-sm"')
}
# Blank lines around the table, so pandoc sees the closing </div> as its own block.
scroll <- function(x) cat('\n<div class="table-scroll">\n\n', x, "\n\n</div>\n\n", sep = "")

# The code a reader sees when unfolding an exhibit: the source of the R functions that
# compute it (read from comparison/R/ at render time, so it cannot drift) and of their
# Python twins in comparison/py/bridge.py (same names).
rdef <- function(fn) {
  f <- get(fn, envir = globalenv()); sr <- attr(f, "srcref")
  l <- as.character(sr); l[1] <- paste0(fn, " <- ", l[1])
  c(sprintf("# comparison/R/%s, lines %d-%d", basename(attr(sr, "srcfile")$filename),
            as.integer(sr)[1], as.integer(sr)[3]), l, "")
}
pydef <- function(fn) {
  l <- readLines("../py/bridge.py", warn = FALSE); i <- grep(paste0("^def ", fn, "\\("), l)
  if (length(i) != 1) return(NULL)
  nxt <- which(seq_along(l) > i & grepl("^[^[:space:]#]", l))
  j <- if (length(nxt)) nxt[1] - 1 else length(l)
  while (j > i && (!nzchar(trimws(l[j])) || grepl("^#", l[j]))) j <- j - 1
  c(sprintf("# comparison/py/bridge.py, lines %d-%d (read-only display)", i, j), l[i:j], "")
}
twin_html <- function(what, r, py) {
  if (is.null(py)) {
    cat(sprintf('\n<details class="code-fold"><summary>R code for %s</summary>\n\n', what),
        "```r\n", paste(r, collapse = "\n"), "\n```\n\n</details>\n\n", sep = "")
    return(invisible())
  }
  cat(sprintf('\n<details class="twin code-fold"><summary><a href="#" class="lang on" data-lang="r">R</a> or <a href="#" class="lang" data-lang="py">Python</a> code for %s</summary>\n\n', what),
      "::: {.lang-r}\n```r\n", paste(r, collapse = "\n"), "\n```\n:::\n\n",
      "::: {.lang-py}\n```python\n", paste(py, collapse = "\n"), "\n```\n:::\n\n</details>\n\n", sep = "")
}
# One fold, one line: "R or Python code for <exhibit>"; the R functions and their twins.
twin_fold <- function(exhibit, fns, py = fns) {
  r <- unlist(lapply(fns, rdef))
  p <- unlist(lapply(py, pydef))
  if (!is.null(p)) p <- c("# The Python twin (comparison/py/bridge.py); it writes comparison/export/py/.", "", p)
  twin_html(exhibit, r, p)
}
```

## Introduction

::: {.report-intro}
![](assets/opa/opa-details.png){.opa-figure}

Proposition 40 would tax Californians worth \$1 billion or more once, at 5% of their net
worth. The [BSZ analysis](../../bsz-analysis/site/) estimates about
`r bsz_round_words` of wealth tax (its Table 5 prints
`r usd(epv("bsz_tab5_row1", "printed_value"), 0)`), or `r usd(eb$bsz_model)` net of the income
tax it adds and loses over `r fmt_input("H", inp$bsz_value[inp$input == "H"])`. The
[JR analysis](../../rjkdc-analysis/site/) finds the state about
**`r usd(-eb$jr_own, 0)`** poorer in today's dollars, net of the income tax lost for ever
(their paper prints an average of `r usd(epv("rauh_nber_npv", "printed_value"))`). Two inputs are among the
three largest both on the explorer's path and averaged over every order: how long the lost
income tax is counted, and the chance the tax survives a court challenge. The third depends on
the order, because the inputs multiply each other: a departure matters more when more wealth
is left to tax. On the explorer's path it is the wealth of billionaires who have already left.
Averaged over every order (the order-free check at the end of [The bridge](#the-bridge)) it is
the share of income tax lost, which shares a large joint effect with the years counted. This
report puts both on one output and walks from one to the other.

<details class="report-fold"><summary>Versions and citations</summary>

Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act, taxes people who lived in California on 1 January
2026 and are worth \$1 billion or more. The tax is 5% of their whole net worth as valued on
31 December 2026. It is payable at once or in five equal yearly installments, and each later
installment carries a deferral charge of 7.5% a year on the unpaid balance (§50301(c)). This
report cites each analysis in its latest version.

The BSZ analysis is Boll, Saez and Zucman, NBER WP 35218 (August 2026). NBER is the National
Bureau of Economic Research, which circulates working papers. Its Table 5 row 1 prints
`r usd(epv("bsz_tab5_row1", "printed_value"), 0)` of wealth tax, reproduced here as
**`r usd(epv("bsz_tab5_row1"))`**. With the income tax the tax changes added in, the net
total is **`r usd(eb$bsz_model)`**.

The JR analysis is Jaros and Rauh, NBER chapter c15504, Tax Policy and the Economy vol. 41
(September 2026). It revises the March 2026 version by Rauh, Jaros, Kearney, Doran and Cosso.
By its own account the tax would collect about
`r usd(pick(k$docs, "nber_headline_revenue"), 0)`, for a net present value of
`r usd(epv("rauh_nber_npv", "printed_value"))`.

Today's dollars (present value) means what money received or lost in future years is worth
now.

</details>

This report is part of the comparison's [Open Policy Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1093/scipol/scaa067) (OPA):

- **Open Output**: [the explorer](explorer/index.html), with the two main estimates on the
  net fiscal effect. Its two panels have one slider per disputed input that moves the
  estimate, from one analysis's value to the other's. The browser computes each panel's
  estimate with `explorer/model.js`, a copy of `score_common()` that a test checks against the
  R values. The explorer's equation shows two of the bridge's nine steps in this report on their own
  (D and q). It adds up the four steps of the loss box (H, f, C and r) into one term, and the
  other three steps into another.
- **Open Analysis**: this document
- **Open Materials**: [the repository folder](https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40/tree/main/comparison), every script, test and data file (guide: [the materials page](materials.html))
:::

**The two main estimates** are the ones each analysis's overview page shows: the BSZ
analysis's net total over 5 years, **`r usd(eb$bsz_model)`** (this OPA's construction from
Table 5 row 1), and the JR analysis's mean net present value in perpetuity,
**`r usd(epv("rauh_nber_npv", "printed_value"))`** as printed (NBER, September 2026) and
**`r usd(eb$jr_own)`** as computed exactly here. On
the common output (b), the net fiscal effect, they are the bridge's two ends. The BSZ end is
the same `r usd(eb$bsz_model)`. The JR number is the exact expectation of the authors' Monte
Carlo, the average computed by formula: `r usd(eb$jr_own, 2)`, the JR end. Jaros and Rauh
print `r usd(epv("rauh_nber_npv", "printed_value"))` from one seeded run of that Monte Carlo (a
run of the random draws started from a fixed seed number, so it gives the same draws every
time). The gap between the two ends,
`r usd(eb$bsz_model - eb$jr_model)`, is what the bridge explains. The arithmetic is in
[The two main estimates](#the-main-estimate).

**Neither analysis reports the other's number, or the gap.** Each keeps its own main estimate
on its own overview page. What this report adds is one definition both can be estimated on,
and an accounting of the distance between them.

**What "reproduced" means here.** The comparison does not re-run either analysis. It reads
each analysis's *export contract*: two files, `inputs.csv` and `outputs.csv`, that each
analysis's own pipeline writes under `export/r/` for others to read. It also reads a short list
of values transcribed from the PDFs with their page (`comparison/data/`). From these it rebuilds
both ends with one estimating function and checks each end against the number its authors
print.

### How to read this report

Every number in running text is computed when this page is rendered, from the files
`comparison/run.R` writes. Open any "code" fold to see the R functions behind an exhibit and
their Python twins (a Python twin: the same computation written a second time in Python and
checked against the R result). Page numbers are PDF pages. The Shapley average, an order-free
check on the bridge, is defined at the end of [The bridge](#the-bridge).

# The common output, and what each analysis reports {#the-common-output}

The BSZ analysis says how much the one-time tax collects. The JR analysis says what the state
gains or loses in present value once income tax lost to billionaires who leave is subtracted.
Before any step of a bridge means anything, both are put on the same two outputs. Output (b)
comes first, because it is the question both main estimates answer:

- **(b) net fiscal effect**: the one-time wealth tax collected, plus extra income tax from
  assets sold to pay the tax, minus the present value of income tax lost to departures over a
  horizon of H years.
- **(a) gross revenue**: the one-time wealth tax collected, the secondary output.

The horizon H is itself disputed. The BSZ analysis argues that the losses should be temporary
and gives five years, the payment period, as an example ("If they last say only 5 years", BSZ
PDF p.27); its Table 5 itself takes no stand on how long they last. The
`r fmt_input("H", inp$bsz_value[inp$input == "H"])` at the BSZ end are this OPA's
reading of that example. The JR analysis counts the losses forever, because it assumes
departed billionaires do not return once the Act permanently lifts the cap on intangible
property taxes (chapter PDF p.32).

[]{#the-discount-rate}The discount rate r is an input of the bridge too, with its own dial
(author decision, 15 October 2026). The BSZ analysis gives no rate. This OPA discounts its
5-year loss at `r r3`, the rate of the BSZ analysis overview and the middle of the JR range
(a scenario). The JR analysis values a growing loss: its rate is r &minus; g, the real
discount rate net of the growth of the lost income tax (chapter eqs. 13-14, PDF p.31). It
draws r &minus; g at random, uniformly between `r r_lo` and `r r_hi` (eq. 18, PDF p.35), and
averages the results. That draw is worth the same as one rate, `r r_jr`, which is the JR value
of the dial. The derivation is short. A perpetuity of 1 a year is worth 1/r at the rate r.
Averaged over the draw it is worth E[1/r] = ln(`r r_hi` / `r r_lo`) / (`r r_hi`
&minus; `r r_lo`) = ln(3)/0.03 = `r formatC(mv("A_inf_jr_draw"), format = "f", digits = 1)`.
That is more than the `r formatC(1 / mv("r_bsz"), format = "f", digits = 1)` it is worth at the
middle rate, `r r3`, because 1/r curves upward, so low rates add more than high rates take
away. The one rate worth the same is r = 1 / E[1/r] = 0.03 / ln(3) =
`r formatC(100 * mv("r_jr"), format = "f", digits = 4)`%, shown as `r r_jr` (a value derived
from the authors' draw). It matches the draw exactly only for a loss that lasts for ever. With
it the common function returns the authors' exact mean.

[]{#conventions}**Conventions.** All amounts are billions of dollars. Present values are as of the date the
wealth tax is assessed, and the first year of lost income tax is counted one year later. The
wealth tax is counted at its face value when assessed (the BSZ analysis values the base on 1
July 2026; the JR analysis's September version grows the base it used in March, the 2025
Forbes list, by `r pct(pick(k$rjkdc$inputs, "nber_growth_rate"))` to 31 December 2026),
undiscounted, as both analyses count it, and the comparison follows them. The Act lets a
taxpayer pay at once or in five yearly installments, each later one with a deferral charge of
7.5% a year on the unpaid balance (§50301(c)). An Optional Deferral Account (§50304) can delay
the tax on illiquid assets. Neither analysis counts either provision, and this OPA does not
estimate them. The lost income tax is a flat yearly amount, discounted at the rate dial's value.
The JR analysis's rate is a real rate net of the growth of the lost tax, r &minus; g (chapter
eqs. 14 and 18), so a flat loss at that rate is the chapter's growing loss. Its code, eq. 18
and its NBER README all draw r &minus; g; one sentence after eq. 19 writes r alone (the JR
analysis's note 3). The BSZ end's `r r3` is the middle of the same draw.

```{r}
#| results: asis
twin_fold("the two analyses on the common output", c("annuity", "score_common", "expected_annuity", "jr_discount_rate", "rauh_nber_expectation"))
```

```{r}
#| results: asis
d <- k$docs
dv <- function(id) as.numeric(d$value[d$input_id == id])
tab <- data.frame(
  Analysis = c("BSZ analysis: Boll, Saez and Zucman, NBER WP 35218, Table 5 row 1 (Aug 2026)",
               "JR analysis: Jaros and Rauh, NBER c15504 (Sep 2026)"),
  `(b) net fiscal effect` = c(money(eb$bsz_model, 1), money(eb$jr_model, 2)),
  `(a) gross revenue` = c(money(ea$bsz_model, 1), money(ea$jr_own, 1)),
  `What the authors print` = c(
    sprintf("%s revenue (PDF p.39); no net figure", money(epv("bsz_tab5_row1", "printed_value"), 0)),
    sprintf("mean NPV %s (one seeded run); revenue 'approximately %s' (p.1)",
            money(epv("rauh_nber_npv", "printed_value"), 1), money(dv("nber_headline_revenue"), 0))),
  check.names = FALSE)
scroll(show(tab))
```

Output (b) for the BSZ analysis is not printed by the paper. It is Table 5 row 1's own three
columns combined here: the `r usd(ea$bsz_model)` revenue, plus
`r usd(ex$meta$value[ex$meta$key == "X_bsz"], 2)` of extra income tax from asset sales, minus
`r usd(ex$meta$value[ex$meta$key == "PV_bsz_own"], 2)`, the present value of five years of
its income tax loss, at `r r3`. For the JR analysis both outputs are the expectation of the
authors' own Monte Carlo, computed exactly rather than by drawing.

# One function, both ends {#the-two-ends}

One function gives both ends of the net fiscal effect: **`r usd(eb$bsz_model)`** at the BSZ
inputs (discounted at `r r3`) and **`r usd(eb$jr_model)`** at the JR inputs (discounted at
`r r_jr`), the JR analysis's own exact mean.

One estimating function, `score_common()`, takes every disputed input as an argument. Each
argument takes either the BSZ analysis's value or the JR analysis's. At the all-BSZ setting
the function must return the BSZ end: Table 5 row 1 on (a), and its net on (b). At the all-JR
setting it must return the exact expectation of the September 2026 version's Monte Carlo, on
both outputs. The draws are independent, so the expectation is the inputs at their means, with
the rate at the one value worth the same as its draw ([above](#the-discount-rate)). The JR
values are those of that version, the latest (its code and person-level file are in the
authors' public repository).

```{r}
# The JR end in closed form (R/model.R rauh_nber_expectation()): the revenue, the share lost and
# the yearly income tax at the means of their uniform draws, and the rate term at the mean of
# 1/(r - g) over its draw. The draws are independent, so the mean of the product is the product
# of the means. Stop if the closed form and the export disagree.
oi0 <- k$rjkdc$inputs
cf_wt <- (0 + pick(oi0, "nber_ceiling_hardcoded")) / 2
cf_f  <- (pick(oi0, "nber_mc_f_min") + pick(oi0, "nber_mc_f_max")) / 2
cf_c  <- (pick(oi0, "rauh_mc_c_min") + pick(oi0, "rauh_mc_c_max")) / 2
cf_a  <- expected_annuity(Inf, pick(oi0, "rauh_mc_r_min"), pick(oi0, "rauh_mc_r_max"))
cf_npv <- cf_wt - cf_f * cf_c * cf_a
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(cf_npv, eb$jr_own)))
# The litigation dial at the JR end (the explorer's note links here): the common function has no
# revenue draw, so q at the JR value turns the ceiling into the draw's mean, E[WT]. Stop if not.
cf_ceil <- pick(oi0, "nber_ceiling_hardcoded")
q_jr <- bridge_inputs(k)$rauh$q
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(score_common(bridge_inputs(k)$rauh)[["a"]], cf_wt)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(q_jr * cf_ceil, cf_wt)))
sgn <- function(x, d) paste0(if (x < 0) "&minus;" else "", formatC(abs(x), format = "f", digits = d))
```

In billions of dollars, with WT the wealth tax, f the share of all billionaires' income tax that is lost,
C the yearly income tax of California's billionaires and r &minus; g the discount rate net of
the loss's growth:

<p class="display-line">E[NPV] = E[WT] &minus; E[f] &times; E[C] &times; E[1/(r &minus; g)]
= `r format(cf_wt)` &minus; `r format(cf_f)` &times; `r format(cf_c)` &times;
`r formatC(cf_a, format = "f", digits = 2)` = `r sgn(cf_npv, 2)`</p>

The `r usd(epv("rauh_nber_npv", "printed_value"))` that the authors print is the average of one
seeded run of the same draws, so it differs from this mean by simulation noise.

[]{#the-litigation-dial}**The litigation dial.** In the line above, E[WT] is where the chance
that the tax survives a court challenge, q, enters the JR end. The authors' Monte Carlo draws
the revenue anywhere between zero (the tax struck down) and the ceiling, `r usd(cf_ceil, 0)`, so
the mean revenue is half the ceiling, `r usd(cf_wt, 0)`. The JR analysis's own explorer has a
litigation dial that reads 1 at the main estimate, because there this draw already halves the
mean revenue. The common function has no revenue draw. So the comparison applies the same half
as q = `r pct(q_jr)` of the ceiling, and its JR end collects the same `r usd(cf_wt, 0)`.

In words, the function computes seven quantities in order.

<details class="report-fold"><summary>The seven quantities, step by step</summary>

Each argument is written as
`score_common()` names it and, where a step of the bridge switches it, followed by that step's
title in quotation marks; `tau`, `m`, `g` and `t_cg` are shared by both ends.

[]{#step-revenue}Steps 1 to 3 give the wealth tax collected, the explorer's
5% × (W − D) × (1 − a) × q. In the code, 5% is `tau`, and W is
`(W_core + W_noncit) * (1 - re)`: the list's wealth with two of the minor inputs. D and q keep
their names, and a is `alpha`.

1. `R0 = tau * (W_core + W_noncit) * (1 - re)`: the revenue with no behavioural response.
   `tau` is the tax rate; `W_core` (the base) and `W_noncit` (the non-US-citizen residents)
   are in billions of dollars ("Forbes source: which list and valuation date", "Non-US-citizen residents");
   `re` is the share of the revenue the real-estate deduction removes ("Real-estate
   deduction").
2. `S = 1 - d_conf`: the share of the base still taxed. `d_conf = D / Wn` is the share of the
   base that had already left ("Billionaires who moved out in time"): `D` is their wealth, valued on
   the Forbes list in use (`lam` picks it), and `Wn` the base net of real estate. The departures
   dial has three stops: none, the BSZ analysis's Table 5 row 3 scenario, which counts four named
   billionaires as having moved in time, and the JR analysis's seven. For the JR analysis, `R0 * S` is its ceiling, the most the tax can collect
   after the seven publicly reported moves.
3. `WT = R0 * (1 - alpha) * S * q`: output (a), the gross one-time revenue, after the avoidance
   allowance `alpha`, a share of the base ("Avoidance and evasion allowance"), weighted by `q`,
   the chance that the Act survives a court challenge (the step "Chance the tax does not
   survive litigation" moves it from 1 to the JR value).
   The JR Monte Carlo draws the revenue anywhere between zero (struck down) and the ceiling;
   the mean of that draw is the ceiling times one half, its `q`.
4. `X = WT * s * g * t_cg`: the extra income tax from assets sold to pay. `s` is the share of
   the tax paid by selling assets ("Extra income tax from selling assets to pay"), `g` the
   capital-gain share of a sale and `t_cg` the top California rate on realized gains.
[]{#step-loss}Steps 5 and 6 give the income tax lost, the explorer's f × C × A(H, r). A(H, r)
is `annuity(r, H)`, about `r formatC(mv("A_5"), format = "f", digits = 1)` for 5 years at `r r3`
and `r formatC(mv("A_inf"), format = "f", digits = 1)` for ever at `r r_jr`.

5. `f = alpha*m + own * L / C + f0`: the share of billionaire income tax lost ("Share of
   billionaire income tax lost"). The first term is the BSZ movers' share (`m` is the part of
   the avoidance allowance that is people leaving California). Under the BSZ rule (`own = 1`)
   the leavers' own income tax, `L` dollars a year as BSZ Table 5 counts it for the people at
   the departures stop, is lost. Under the JR rule (`own = 0`) a flat share `f0` of all
   billionaires' income tax is lost, set above the share of wealth that left (the JR analysis's
   independent draw of 30% to 60%). At the middle stop the BSZ end reproduces Table 5 row 3 in
   all three columns.
6. `PV = f * C * annuity(r, H)`: the present value of the lost income tax. `C` is
   billionaires' annual California income tax, in billions of dollars a year ("Billionaires'
   annual CA income tax"), lost for `H` years ("How long the income tax loss lasts"; for ever
   at the JR end); `annuity(r, H) = (1 - (1 + r)^-H) / r` is what 1 a year for `H` years is
   worth today at the discount rate `r` ("Discount rate for the lost income tax": `r r3` at the
   BSZ end, `r r_jr` at the JR end).
7. `NET = WT + X - PV`: output (b), the net fiscal effect.

</details>

The BSZ end matches the number its authors print, up to rounding. The JR end matches the
exact mean of the authors' Monte Carlo, and that mean matches their printed number up to the
sampling error of one run.

<details class="report-fold"><summary>The endpoint checks</summary>


```{r}
#| results: asis
twin_fold("the endpoint checks", c("bridge_inputs", "score_common"))
```

```{r}

e2 <- ep[match(c("bsz_net_constructed", "bsz_tab5_row1", "rauh_nber_npv", "rauh_nber_revenue_mc"), ep$endpoint_id), ]
scroll(show(data.frame(
  End = esc(e2$description),
  `Computed here` = vapply(e2$value, function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 3), ""),
  `Printed` = ifelse(is.na(e2$printed_value), "not printed", formatC(e2$printed_value, format = "f", digits = 1)),
  Where = ifelse(is.na(e2$printed_where), "", e2$printed_where),
  `Difference` = ifelse(is.na(e2$abs_diff_printed), "", formatC(e2$abs_diff_printed, format = "f", digits = 3)),
  check.names = FALSE)))
```

The BSZ differences are rounding of the printed number. The JR difference is the sampling
error of the authors' one seeded run: the exact mean of the Monte Carlo, `r usd(eb$jr_own, 2)`,
rounds to `r usd(eb$jr_own)`, while their run of it prints
`r usd(epv("rauh_nber_npv", "printed_value"))`.

</details>

## The two main estimates {#the-main-estimate}

```{r}
bi  <- bridge_inputs(k)                       # the two input vectors, from the contracts
sup <- bi$sup
v_sup <- score_common(sup)                    # the BSZ end, both outputs
oi <- k$rjkdc$inputs
nber <- rauh_nber_expectation(wt_min = 0, wt_max = pick(oi, "nber_ceiling_hardcoded"),
                              f_min = pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_min"), f_max = pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_max"),
                              c_min = pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_min"), c_max = pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_max"),
                              r_min = pick(oi, "rauh_mc_r_min"), r_max = pick(oi, "rauh_mc_r_max"))
v_rj <- score_common(bi$rauh)                 # the JR end, both outputs
rj_main <- eb$jr_own                              # the JR main estimate: the exact expectation (author decision 2026-10-15)
rj_run <- epv("rauh_nber_npv", "contract_value")    # the authors' seeded run, as the JR pipeline reproduces it
f_mid <- (pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_min") + pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_max")) / 2
c_mid <- (pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_min") + pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_max")) / 2
a_inf <- expected_annuity(Inf, pick(oi, "rauh_mc_r_min"), pick(oi, "rauh_mc_r_max"))   # E[1/r] over the draw
a_one <- annuity(bi$rauh$r, Inf)                                                        # 1/r at r_jr: the same
gap_b <- v_sup[["b"]] - v_rj[["b"]]
gap <- v_sup[["a"]] - v_rj[["a"]]
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(v_sup[["b"]], eb$bsz_model)), isTRUE(all.equal(v_rj[["b"]], eb$jr_model)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(nber[["b"]], eb$jr_own)), abs(v_rj[["b"]] - nber[["b"]]) < 1e-9,
          isTRUE(all.equal(a_one, a_inf)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(v_sup[["a"]], ea$bsz_model)), isTRUE(all.equal(nber[["a"]], ea$jr_own)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(v_rj[["a"]], nber[["a"]])))
```

The BSZ main estimate is **`r usd(eb$bsz_model)`** and the JR main estimate
**`r usd(rj_main)`**. On the common output the two ends are
`r usd(eb$bsz_model)` and `r usd(eb$jr_model)`, a gap of **`r usd(eb$bsz_model - eb$jr_model)`**.
The JR main estimate is the JR end: the exact mean of the authors' Monte Carlo.
The BSZ net total is this OPA's choice, not the authors'. Their own headline is the wealth tax
alone, Table 5 row 1 (printed `r usd(epv("bsz_tab5_row1", "printed_value"), 0)`), and the
[BSZ analysis overview](../../bsz-analysis/site/) explains the choice.

<details class="report-fold"><summary>Steps 1 to 4, and output (a)</summary>

**Step 1: the BSZ main estimate, the BSZ end on (b).** At the all-BSZ inputs, the wealth tax
is the tax rate times the base, less the avoidance allowance. The base is the
`r usd(sup$W_core + sup$W_noncit, 0)` that Forbes lists for California's billionaires on 1 July
2026, the non-US-citizen residents (`r usd(sup$W_noncit, 0)`) included. The BSZ analysis
applies no real-estate deduction and removes no named leaver from the base. Its
`r pct(sup$alpha)` avoidance allowance includes the `r pct(sup$alpha * sup$m)` of billionaires
who left before 1 January 2026 (BSZ PDF p.24), which is where its income tax loss comes from.
So the wealth tax is `r pct(sup$tau)` &times;
`r usd(sup$W_core + sup$W_noncit, 0)` &times; (1 &minus; `r pct(sup$alpha)`) =
`r usd(v_sup[["a"]], 3)`, which is Table 5 row 1 (printed
`r usd(epv("bsz_tab5_row1", "printed_value"), 0)`, PDF p.39). Output (b) adds
`r usd(v_sup[["X"]], 3)` of extra income tax from assets sold to pay and subtracts
`r usd(v_sup[["PV"]], 3)`, five years of the `r usd(v_sup[["annual_loss"]], 3)` annual
income tax loss discounted at `r r3`: **`r usd(v_sup[["b"]], 3)`**, shown as
`r usd(v_sup[["b"]])`, the BSZ analysis overview's main estimate.

**Step 2: the JR main estimate, and the JR end on (b).** In the Monte Carlo of Jaros and
Rauh's NBER version the revenue is drawn uniformly between zero and
`r usd(pick(oi, "nber_ceiling_hardcoded"), 0)`, the share of all billionaires' income tax that is lost
between `r pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_min")` and `r pick(oi, "nber_mc_f_max")`, the annual income tax
between `r usd(pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_min"))` and `r usd(pick(oi, "rauh_mc_c_max"))`, and the
discount rate net of the loss's growth, r &minus; g, between `r r_lo` and `r r_hi`, all
independently. The mean net present value is
therefore `r usd(nber[["a"]], 1)` &minus; `r f_mid` &times; `r usd(c_mid, 3)` &times;
`r formatC(a_inf, format = "f", digits = 3)` (the average of 1/r, or 1/r at `r r_jr`) =
**`r usd(nber[["b"]], 3)`**, the JR end on (b). The authors print `r usd(epv("rauh_nber_npv", "printed_value"))`
from one seeded run of the same Monte Carlo, which the JR pipeline reproduces as
`r usd(rj_run, 3)`. The comparison's pages use the exact mean as the JR main estimate, shown
as `r usd(rj_main)`.

**Step 3: the gap on (b).** `r usd(v_sup[["b"]], 3)` &minus; (`r usd(v_rj[["b"]], 3)`) =
**`r usd(gap_b, 3)`**, shown as `r usd(gap_b)`.

**Step 4: where the gap comes from.** The next section splits it into one step per dial of
the explorer. The steps add up to `r usd(sum(dp$change), 3, TRUE)`, the gap read from the BSZ
end: the common function returns both ends exactly, and the steps go from one to the other.

**On output (a)**, the secondary setting, the two ends are the wealth tax alone:
`r usd(v_sup[["a"]], 3)` and the NBER expected revenue, `r usd(nber[["a"]], 1)` (the midpoint
of zero and `r usd(pick(oi, "nber_ceiling_hardcoded"), 0)`; the authors print "approximately
`r usd(dv("nber_headline_revenue"), 0)`", p.1). The gap is `r usd(gap, 3)`. The order-free
check at the end of the next section splits it too.

</details>

```{r}
b_a <- br[br$horizon_setting == "own" & br$output == "a", ]
b_b <- br[br$horizon_setting == "own" & br$output == "b", ]
stopifnot(abs(sum(b_b$shapley) + gap_b) < 1e-9, abs(sum(b_a$shapley) + gap) < 1e-9,
          abs(sum(dp$change) + gap_b) < 1e-9,
          max(abs(own$jr_residual)) < 1e-9)
# The introduction names the three largest steps of the dial path in words; stop if they change.
top3p <- dp[order(-abs(dp$change)), ][1:3, ]
stopifnot(identical(top3p$step_id, c("horizon", "litigation_survival", "confirmed_departures")))
```

```{r}
#| results: asis
twin_fold("the two main estimates", c("bridge_inputs", "score_common", "rauh_nber_expectation"))
```

# The bridge, step by step {#the-bridge}

The bridge follows the explorer's dials. Start from the BSZ panel, where every dial is at the
BSZ value, and move each dial to its far end (the JR value), in the order of the explorer's
equation. That order is D, then q, then the four loss-box dials (f, C, H and r), then W, a and
the minor switch. Each step is what one dial changes. The nine steps take the BSZ end, `r usd(dp$from[1])`, to the JR end,
`r usd(dp$to[nrow(dp)])`, exactly. On this path, three of them make most of the `r usd(gap_b)` gap: how long
the lost income tax is counted (`r usd(dp$change[dp$step_id == "horizon"], 1, TRUE)`), the
chance the tax does not survive litigation
(`r usd(dp$change[dp$step_id == "litigation_survival"], 1, TRUE)`) and the billionaires who
moved out in time (`r usd(dp$change[dp$step_id == "confirmed_departures"], 1, TRUE)`). The other
`r nrow(dp) - 3` together add
`r usd(sum(dp$change[!dp$step_id %in% top3p$step_id]), 1, TRUE)`.

The inputs interact, so a step's size depends on where the other dials stand when it moves.
A departure matters more when the base is larger, for example. This path uses the equation's
order, left to right, so a reader can reproduce every step with the dials
([The explorer's equation](#the-equation) below). An order-free check, the Shapley average,
closes this section.

```{r}
#| results: asis
twin_fold("the bridge table and the figure", c("slider_inputs", "slider_value", "dial_path"))
```

```{r}
#| results: asis
# One row per dial in the path's order (the equation's); the minor switch's row joins its three inputs.
path_texts <- function(id) {
  ids <- dial_ids(id); tx <- lapply(ids, function(i) step_texts(inp, i))
  st <- steps[match(ids, steps$step_id), ]
  list(row = paste(st$disputes_row, collapse = ", "), kind = paste(unique(st$kind), collapse = ", "),
       bsz = paste(vapply(tx, `[[`, "", "bsz"), collapse = "; "),
       rjkdc = paste(vapply(tx, `[[`, "", "rjkdc"), collapse = "; "))
}
pt <- lapply(dp$step_id, path_texts)
# a signed amount stays on one line: show() wraps it (nobr_amounts() in the setup)
path_rows <- data.frame(
  Dial = ifelse(dp$step_id == "minor_inputs", esc(dp$title),
                sprintf("<i>%s</i>, %s", dp$symbol, esc(dp$title))),
  `DISPUTES row` = vapply(pt, `[[`, "", "row"), Kind = vapply(pt, `[[`, "", "kind"),
  `BSZ value` = vapply(pt, `[[`, "", "bsz"), `JR value` = vapply(pt, `[[`, "", "rjkdc"),
  Change = vapply(dp$change, money, "", digits = 2, signed = TRUE),
  `Running value` = vapply(dp$to, money, "", digits = 2), check.names = FALSE)
blank <- function(label, change, run) data.frame(Dial = label, `DISPUTES row` = "", Kind = "",
  `BSZ value` = "", `JR value` = "", Change = change, `Running value` = run, check.names = FALSE)
cat("\n**Output (b), net fiscal effect, each analysis's own horizon.** The horizon dial moves from the BSZ analysis's 5 years to a perpetuity.\n\n")
scroll(show(rbind(blank("<b>BSZ end, (b)</b>", "", money(dp$from[1], 2)), path_rows,
                  blank("Sum of the steps", money(sum(dp$change), 2, TRUE), ""),
                  blank("<b>JR end, (b), the JR main estimate</b>", "", money(eb$jr_own, 2)))))
```

Reading the table: the horizon step is the largest because it moves after f and C, when the
share lost and the yearly income tax are already at the JR values, and a perpetuity multiplies
that annual loss. One step
raises the number. The JR analysis applies no avoidance allowance beyond migration, so dropping
the BSZ analysis's `r pct(sup$alpha)` adds
`r usd(dp$change[dp$step_id == "avoidance"], 1, TRUE)`. The rate step,
`r usd(dp$change[dp$step_id == "discount_rate"], 1, TRUE)`, is what the authors' random draw
of the rate (r &minus; g) adds to a loss that lasts for ever: at `r r_jr` a perpetuity is worth
`r formatC(mv("A_inf"), format = "f", digits = 1)` a year's loss, against
`r formatC(1 / mv("r_bsz"), format = "f", digits = 1)` at `r r3`.


```{r}
# The explorer's equation (its footnote 2 links here; author request 2026-10-17: the explorer's
# notes are three sentences at most, the rest is here). et: how the four terms group the nine
# steps (R/site.R eq_terms()). q_first: what q would take if moved first, as in footnote 2.
# The loss term along the path, and the share lost there, against the two analyses' own present
# values of the lost income tax.
et <- eq_terms(dp)
loss_ids <- c("income_loss_share", "income_level", "horizon", "discount_rate")
q_path <- dp$change[dp$step_id == "litigation_survival"]
q_first <- local({ s <- sup; s$q <- bi$rauh$q; score_common(s)[["b"]] - score_common(sup)[["b"]] })
at_path <- function(ids) {
  pos <- setNames(lapply(ids, slider_max), ids)
  score_common(slider_inputs(bi$sup, bi$rauh, pos, bi$ladder))
}
before_loss <- at_path(c("confirmed_departures", "litigation_survival"))
after_loss <- at_path(c("confirmed_departures", "litigation_survival", loss_ids))
loss_term <- sum(dp$change[dp$step_id %in% loss_ids])
movers <- sup$alpha * sup$m
stopifnot(length(q_path) == 1, q_first < q_path,
          abs(after_loss[["PV"]] - before_loss[["PV"]] + loss_term) < 1e-9,
          isTRUE(all.equal(after_loss[["f"]], v_rj[["f"]] + movers)),
          -loss_term > v_rj[["PV"]] - v_sup[["PV"]],
          abs(round(eb$bsz_model, 2) + sum(round(et$terms$change, 2)) - round(eb$jr_model, 2)) < 1e-9)
```

[]{#the-equation}**The explorer's equation.** The equation at the top of the explorer walks this
path and groups its `r et$n_words` steps into four terms. `r et$note` `r et$loss_order` The
four amounts, rounded to two decimals, add up exactly from `r usd(eb$bsz_model, 2)` to
`r usd(eb$jr_model, 2)`. The equation prints its two ends at one decimal,
`r usd(eb$bsz_model)` and `r usd(eb$jr_model)`, the figures of the two main estimates.

The equation adds up only along this path. In another order the same dials split the gap
differently among the terms. Moved first, q would take `r usd(q_first, 2)` instead of
`r usd(q_path, 2)`. With D still at the BSZ value, the revenue still counts the tax on the
billionaires who already left, so halving it halves that tax too.

The Apply buttons under the equation work from left to right. A term can be applied once every
term to its left is applied, and undone once every term to its right is undone, so each press
changes the BSZ panel by that term's amount. Reset and Apply all always work. The Walk the path
button in each panel moves one dial per press along the same path. The JR panel's button walks
it backwards, from the last term to the first.

[]{#lost-income-tax-scale}For scale, the lost income tax itself is worth
`r usd(v_rj[["PV"]])` today in the JR analysis and `r usd(v_sup[["PV"]])` in the BSZ
analysis. The equation's lost income tax term, `r usd(abs(loss_term), 2)`, is neither. It is the
change along the path, from `r usd(before_loss[["PV"]])` to `r usd(after_loss[["PV"]])`. It ends
above the JR analysis's `r usd(v_rj[["PV"]])` because the avoidance dial, a, has not moved yet.
Until it does, the share lost is `r pct(after_loss[["f"]])` instead of `r pct(v_rj[["f"]])`,
because it still holds the BSZ movers' `r pct(movers)`.

<details class="report-fold" id="the-shapley-check"><summary><span id="order-free-check"></span>An order-free check: the Shapley average</summary>

The path's steps depend on the order the dials move in. The same dial moved earlier or later
changes the estimate by a different amount, because the inputs multiply each other. The
Shapley average removes the order. It takes every order the inputs could be switched in and
averages each input's step over them. Its steps also add up to the gap, so it checks the path
without choosing an order. Here each step switches one input from the BSZ value to the JR
value of its September 2026 version (the share-lost step switches its two arguments together).
The tables show two answers:

- **Shapley values**. Each step's switch is averaged over
  all `r format(factorial(nrow(steps)), big.mark = ",")` orders of the
  `r nrow(steps)` steps. The code computes this exactly, by estimating the model at every one
  of the `r format(2^nrow(steps), big.mark = ",")` subsets of switched inputs. The steps then
  add up to the total gap whatever order they are read in.
- **One order**: a single sequence, the one Hoopes (2026) reads in (see
  [below](#the-hoopes-comparison)).

```{r}
#| results: asis
twin_fold("the Shapley tables", c("switch_inputs", "shapley_bridge", "sequential_bridge"))
```

```{r}
#| results: asis
bt <- function(o) {
  b <- br[br$horizon_setting == "own" & br$output == o, ]
  b <- b[match(steps$step_id, b$step_id), ]
  tx <- lapply(b$step_id, function(id) step_texts(inp, id))
  e <- own[own$output == o, ]
  rows <- data.frame(
    Step = esc(b$title), `DISPUTES row` = b$disputes_row, Kind = b$kind,
    `BSZ value` = vapply(tx, `[[`, "", "bsz"),
    `JR value` = vapply(tx, `[[`, "", "rjkdc"),
    Shapley = vapply(b$shapley, money, "", digits = 2, signed = TRUE),
    `One order` = vapply(b$sequential, money, "", digits = 2, signed = TRUE),
    check.names = FALSE)
  extra <- data.frame(
    Step = "Sum of the steps", `DISPUTES row` = "", Kind = "", `BSZ value` = "", `JR value` = "",
    Shapley = money(sum(b$shapley), 2, TRUE), `One order` = money(sum(b$sequential), 2, TRUE),
    check.names = FALSE)
  top <- data.frame(Step = sprintf("<b>BSZ end, (%s)</b>", o), `DISPUTES row` = "", Kind = "", `BSZ value` = "",
                    `JR value` = "", Shapley = money(e$bsz_model, 2), `One order` = money(e$bsz_model, 2), check.names = FALSE)
  bot <- data.frame(Step = sprintf("<b>JR end, (%s)</b>", o), `DISPUTES row` = "", Kind = "", `BSZ value` = "",
                    `JR value` = "", Shapley = money(e$jr_model, 2), `One order` = money(e$jr_model, 2), check.names = FALSE)
  scroll(show(rbind(top, rows, extra, bot)))
}
cat("\n**Output (b), net fiscal effect, each analysis's own horizon.** The horizon step switches from the BSZ analysis's 5 years to a perpetuity.\n\n"); bt("b")
```

```{r}
# The joint effect of two inputs, which the Shapley average splits equally between them: the
# common function's second difference, read from the switchboard (output (b), own horizons;
# bit i-1 of mask is step i of bridge_steps()). At the BSZ values it is
# v(i,j) - v(i) - v(j) + v(none); at the JR values the same, both moved back from the all-JR mix.
sb <- read_csv_plain(file.path(root, "comparison", "export", "r", "switchboard.csv"))
sb <- sb[sb$output == "b" & sb$horizon_setting == "own", ]
sv <- function(m) sb$value[sb$mask == m]
bit <- function(id) 2^(match(id, steps$step_id) - 1)
all_on <- 2^nrow(steps) - 1
joint <- function(i, j, at_jr = FALSE) {
  a <- bit(i); b <- bit(j)
  if (at_jr) sv(all_on) - sv(all_on - a) - sv(all_on - b) + sv(all_on - a - b)
  else sv(a + b) - sv(a) - sv(b) + sv(0)
}
fh_bsz <- joint("income_loss_share", "horizon")
fh_jr <- joint("income_loss_share", "horizon", at_jr = TRUE)
# The text calls the share lost and the years counted the largest pair: check every pair.
pairs <- combn(steps$step_id, 2)
stopifnot(length(fh_bsz) == 1, length(fh_jr) == 1,
          all(abs(fh_bsz) >= abs(apply(pairs, 2, function(p) joint(p[1], p[2]))) - 1e-9),
          all(abs(fh_jr) >= abs(apply(pairs, 2, function(p) joint(p[1], p[2], at_jr = TRUE))) - 1e-9))
```

Reading the (b) table: the three largest Shapley steps are
```{r}
#| results: asis
top3b <- b_b[order(-abs(b_b$shapley)), ][1:3, ]
cat(paste(sprintf("%s (%s)", tolower(top3b$title), usd(top3b$shapley, 1, TRUE)), collapse = "; "), ".", sep = "")
```
The horizon is the largest step read in Hoopes's order
(`r usd(b_b$sequential[b_b$step_id == "horizon"], 1, TRUE)`, switched last, when the loss is
already JR-sized) but `r usd(b_b$shapley[b_b$step_id == "horizon"], 1, TRUE)` averaged over
orders, because a perpetuity multiplies whatever annual loss the other inputs imply.
The Shapley average splits each interaction equally between the inputs that create it. The
largest is between the share lost and the years counted: at the BSZ values, moving both
changes the estimate by `r usd(fh_bsz, 1, TRUE)` more than moving each alone
(`r usd(fh_jr, 1, TRUE)` at the JR values), and half of it sits in each one's average.
One step raises the number: the JR analysis applies no avoidance allowance beyond migration,
so dropping the BSZ analysis's `r pct(sup$alpha)` adds
`r usd(b_b$shapley[b_b$step_id == "avoidance"], 1, TRUE)` on (b) and
`r usd(b_a$shapley[b_a$step_id == "avoidance"], 1, TRUE)` on (a).

<details class="report-fold"><summary>Output (a), gross revenue</summary>



## Which revenue of the JR analysis the steps reach {#which-revenue}

The September 2026 version prints two revenue figures. On output (a) the steps reach the one
consistent with its mean NPV, the expected revenue in the same Monte Carlo, because it is the
revenue that NPV assumes. Using the other would add a further step of the size shown.

point); row 7 has two parts here, and two rows cover inputs the crosswalk does not list. In the source columns, GGSS is the

# The Hoopes comparison {#the-hoopes-comparison}

Jeffrey Hoopes, "Galle v Rauh: Comparing Two Revenue Estimates for California Billionaire
Taxation" (SSRN 6428578; SSRN is a preprint site), is the one published comparison of the two
estimates. It compares their earlier versions: the February 2026 text of the GGSS expert
report, on which the BSZ analysis builds, and the March 2026 version of the JR analysis. His Figure 2 (p.6) is a
waterfall from the "Galle estimate" to "Rauh net fiscal effect". It
prints no values, so his column below is read off the chart with
`comparison/tools/digitize_hoopes_fig2.py`. The script fits the chart's dollar scale to its
axis ticks, and the fitted scale misses a tick by at most
`r usd(as.numeric(k$hoopes$tick_fit_max_resid[1]), 1)`. Beside his column is the bridge read
in his order, ending at the JR analysis's September 2026 version, which postdates his note.
The list below gives every difference between the two.

```{r}
#| results: asis
twin_fold("the Hoopes comparison", "build_all")
```

```{r}
#| results: asis
hz <- ex$hoopes
scroll(show(data.frame(
  `Hoopes Figure 2 bar` = {lab <- k$hoopes$step_label[match(hz$step_id, k$hoopes$step_id)]; ifelse(is.na(lab), "(no bar)", lab)},
  `Hoopes (read off the chart)` = ifelse(is.na(hz$hoopes), "none",
    paste0(vapply(hz$hoopes, function(x) if (is.na(x)) "" else money(x, 1, TRUE), "") |>
             replace(hz$step_id == "galle_estimate", money(hz$hoopes[hz$step_id == "galle_estimate"], 1)),
           ifelse(is.na(hz$hoopes_uncertainty), "", paste0(" &plusmn; ", formatC(hz$hoopes_uncertainty, format = "f", digits = 1))))),
  `Ours, one order` = vapply(seq_along(hz$ours), function(i) { x <- hz$ours[i]
    if (is.na(x)) "none" else money(x, if (abs(x) < 0.05) 4 else 1, hz$step_id[i] != "galle_estimate") }, ""),
  `Our steps` = esc(hz$our_steps), check.names = FALSE)))
```

Our column follows Hoopes's construction. Its revenue rows are steps on output (a), starting
from the BSZ wealth tax (`r usd(ea$bsz_model)`), and its last row adds the JR analysis's whole
income tax loss. The "One order" column of the (b) table in [the order-free
check](#order-free-check) reads the same order on the net fiscal effect, so its sizes differ.

The "Galle estimate" bar is clipped by the chart's frame at
`r usd(hz$hoopes[hz$step_id == "galle_estimate"], 0)`; its value is taken from the note's text
(p.3), so the reading uncertainty printed with it is the digitizer's default for every bar,
not a measurement.

The note discloses two things. Hoopes states his priors: "To lay my cards on the table, I
believe that the world is complicated, and that when possible, empirical analysis should be
done in as detailed a way as possible" (p.2). He also thanks "David Gamage for encouraging me
to read both of these analyses carefully and compare the two" (p.1). Gamage is a GGSS
co-author.

### Every difference

```{r}
#| results: asis
# hoopes_differences() is in R/site.R; a dollar sign in markdown starts a formula, so escape it,
# and a signed amount stays on one line
cat(paste0("- ", gsub("$", "\\$", nobr_amounts(hoopes_differences(ex, k)), fixed = TRUE)), sep = "\n")
cat("\n")
```

# Every input, by origin {#every-input-by-origin}

The OPA framework sorts every input by where it comes from: **data** (settled by observable
facts), **research** (a published estimate), **guesswork** (an assumption with no data or study
behind it, legal judgements included) and **scenario** (a choice of which world is
estimated). This OPA adds **derived** (computed from the analysis's own inputs) and
**guesswork on data** (a judgement applied to observed facts). Each bridge step carries one of
these kinds (the tables above); a kind written "A vs B" is A for the BSZ value and B for the JR
value. A kind says what evidence is behind a value, not whether the quantity itself can be
observed. The values the comparison transcribes from the PDFs
itself, because neither contract carries them, are in `comparison/data/document-inputs.csv`.

<details class="report-fold"><summary>The transcribed inputs</summary>


```{r}
#| results: asis
twin_fold("reading the inputs", c("read_contracts", "pick"))
```

```{r}
#| results: asis
dd <- k$docs[order(k$docs$label, k$docs$side), ]
# reader-facing names for the side keys (the analysis is called JR in prose; rjkdc is the key)
side_label <- c(bsz = "BSZ", rjkdc = "JR", neutral = "Neutral")
scroll(show(data.frame(
  Origin = dd$label, Analysis = ifelse(dd$side %in% names(side_label), side_label[dd$side], dd$side),
  Input = esc(dd$description),
  Value = paste(format(dd$value, drop0trailing = TRUE), dd$unit), Source = esc(dd$source),
  check.names = FALSE)))
cnt <- table(k$docs$label)
cat(sprintf("\n%d transcribed inputs: %s.\n", nrow(k$docs),
            paste(sprintf("%s %d", names(cnt), as.integer(cnt)), collapse = ", ")))
```

</details>

# What reproduces {#what-reproduces}

```{r}
pdir <- file.path(root, "comparison", "export", "py")
py_ok <- dir.exists(pdir)
maxdiff <- if (py_ok) max(vapply(c("ends", "bridge", "endpoints", "dial_path"), function(f) {
  r <- read_csv_plain(file.path(root, "comparison", "export", "r", paste0(f, ".csv")))
  p <- read_csv_plain(file.path(pdir, paste0(f, ".csv")))
  key <- intersect(c("horizon_setting", "output", "step_id", "endpoint_id"), names(r))
  p <- p[match(do.call(paste, r[key]), do.call(paste, p[key])), ]
  cols <- setdiff(names(r)[vapply(r, is.numeric, TRUE)], "sequential_rank")
  max(vapply(cols, function(cc) max(abs(r[[cc]] - as.numeric(p[[cc]])), na.rm = TRUE), 0))
}, 0)) else NA
```

- **Both ends.** At the all-BSZ inputs the estimating function returns BSZ Table 5 row 1
  exactly (`r usd(ea$bsz_model, 3)`), and its net on (b) (`r usd(eb$bsz_model, 3)`). At the
  inputs of the JR analysis's September 2026 version it returns that version's exact expected
  revenue on (a), `r usd(ea$jr_own, 3)`. It uses the script's ceiling literal, 72, rather
  than the 72.05 the person-level file sums to (the JR analysis's note 4), so that the two
  agree exactly. On (b), with the rate at `r r_jr` (1 / E[1/r] over the authors' draw), it
  returns the authors' exact Monte Carlo mean, `r usd(eb$jr_own, 3)`, to 1e-9, against the
  printed `r usd(epv("rauh_nber_npv", "printed_value"))` from one seeded run.
  `test-endpoints.R` checks both, and that one over `r r_jr` equals the average of 1/r over the draw.
- **The bridge is the explorer's own.** `test-dial-path.R` checks that the nine steps of the
  dial path add up to the gap, and that each equals the difference between two explorer values
  in both panels, in R and in `model.js`.
- **The code does what the method says.** Shapley values sum to the gap by construction;
  `test-shapley.R` checks that ours do in every horizon setting and for both outputs, and that
  they equal a brute-force average over orders. This is a check of the code, not a finding
  about the analyses.
- **R and Python agree.** The Python twin writes the same tables;
  the largest difference on the ends, the bridge, the dial path and the endpoints is
  `r if (py_ok) formatC(maxdiff, format = "e", digits = 1) else "not checked (run comparison/py/bridge.py)"`
  (`test-parity.R` requires 1e-9).
- **Not reproduced.** The comparison does not re-run either analysis: it takes each
  analysis's export contract as given, and each analysis's own reproduction is on its overview
  page.

# Reproducing this document

```sh
Rscript comparison/run.R                 # exports (R and Python), the overview page and the explorer
Rscript comparison/tests/testthat.R      # the test suite
cd comparison/site && quarto render repro.qmd
```

The setup code below reads the exports and defines the helpers every exhibit uses.

```{r}
twin_html("the setup",
  grep("^#\\|", knitr::knit_code$get("setup"), value = TRUE, invert = TRUE),
  c("# The page is built with R, so the Python twin has no setup here: it runs on its own.",

    "#",
    "#   python3 comparison/py/bridge.py      # writes comparison/export/py/",
    "#",
    "# export/py/ holds the same tables this report reads from export/r/, and",
    "# comparison/tests/testthat/test-parity.R checks every number against R's to 1e-9.",
```

```{=html}
// A link to an anchor inside a fold (the explorer's "more" links, #step-revenue and
// #step-loss) opens the fold first.
function openTo(id) {
  var el = id && document.getElementById(decodeURIComponent(id));
  if (!el) return;
  for (var d = el.closest("details"); d; d = d.parentElement.closest("details")) d.open = true;
  el.scrollIntoView();
}
window.addEventListener("hashchange", function () { openTo(location.hash.slice(1)); });
openTo(location.hash.slice(1));
document.querySelectorAll("details.twin > summary a.lang").forEach(function (a) {
  a.addEventListener("click", function (e) {
    e.preventDefault(); e.stopPropagation();
    var d = a.closest("details"); var py = a.dataset.lang === "py";
    if (d.open && d.classList.contains("show-py") === py) { d.open = false; return; }
    d.open = true; d.classList.toggle("show-py", py);
    d.querySelectorAll("summary a.lang").forEach(function (x) { x.classList.toggle("on", x === a); });
  });
});
</script>
```
